clue.text: Insect after vegetables for Hamlet's slave

indicators.note: after says the insect comes behind the vegetables in the answer

parts.note: peas are green vegetables
an ant is an insect

explanation.surface: A bug comes after the greens, served up for a Shakespearean servant.
explanation.walkthrough: Hamlet calls himself 'a rogue and peasant slave' in his soliloquy, so this is the word Hamlet attaches to slave.
explanation.definitionFit: In his soliloquy Hamlet berates himself as a 'rogue and peasant slave', so the lowly label belongs to that slave.

clue.text: Appetising, as in drink

indicators.note: in places the word for 'as' within the drink

parts.note: a pint is a drink, typically of beer
qua is Latin for 'as', in the capacity of

explanation.surface: Something tasty, as one finds in a glass of something.
explanation.definitionFit: Piquant food has a pleasantly sharp, stimulating taste that whets the appetite.

clue.text: Far from 7, with a preference — to imprison rotten cad Kevin

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: to imprison means the preference holds the scrambled letters inside it

parts.note: a liking is a preference

indicators.note: rotten signals the letters of cad and Kevin are spoilt into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone with a fondness for locking up a nasty bounder called Kevin, not dead at all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rotten' rearranges the cad's name and 'to imprison' tucks the result into the fondness word; the cross-reference points to entry 7, the down answer meaning utterly lifeless.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means vigorously active, the opposite of the utterly lifeless state described by entry 7.

clue.text: One putting clock back arrives without carriage

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so the abbreviation wraps the carriage

parts.note: arr is the timetable abbreviation for arrives
a chaise is a light horse-drawn carriage

explanation.surface: Someone turning back the clock turns up with no transport.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' looks like 'lacking' but here has its old sense of outside, so the abbreviation wraps the carriage.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaiser imitates the ways of the past, figuratively turning the clock back to old styles.

clue.text: Shy boy's instincts

parts.note: Tim is a boy's name
the id is the instinctive part of the psyche in Freudian theory

explanation.surface: A bashful lad's gut feelings.
explanation.definitionFit: Shy and timid are synonyms for lacking confidence with others.

clue.text: Comic to be counted?

definitions.meaning: a comedian who performs solo routines before an audience
the idiom '... and be counted' means declare oneself openly

explanation.surface: A comedian wondering whether to be included in the tally.
explanation.definitionFit: A stand-up is a solo comedian; one must stand up and be counted to declare one's position.

clue.text: More to pay for tea during boiling

indicators.note: during puts the tea in the middle of the boiling

parts.note: a surge is a boiling or seething rush, as of the sea
char is a British slang word for tea

explanation.surface: An extra charge for your cuppa while the kettle boils.
explanation.definitionFit: A surcharge is an additional amount added to the price to be paid.

clue.text: Prize poster brought about considerable hostility

indicators.note: brought about means the poster is put round the hostility

parts.note: an ad, advertisement, can be a poster
war is hostility on a large scale

explanation.surface: A prize-winning poster stirred up a lot of bad feeling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brought about' reads as 'caused', but it means the advert goes about WAR.
explanation.definitionFit: An award is a prize given in recognition of merit.

clue.text: A tragic love in Deck 1, kidnapped by Scottish fiend, with no hope of revival

indicators.note: kidnapped by means the Scottish devil carries all of that inside him

parts.note: deil is the Scots word for the devil

indicators.note: in puts the tragic love inside the decoration

parts.note: to deck is to adorn
taken as written
tragic suggests sad
love is zero in tennis, the letter O
the figure one gives A

explanation.surface: A sad romance aboard ship, snatched by a Scottish demon, ends with no chance of coming back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Deck 1' looks like a ship's deck but is a verb plus a number; the inner container sits inside the Scots devil between his second and third letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes something utterly dead, beyond any possibility of being revived.

clue.text: Setter drops in, keeping judge from monitor

indicators.note: keeping means what is left holds the judge inside it
drops means the word 'in' is let fall from the setting agent

parts.note: pectin is the setting agent in jam
taken as written
a ref, referee, judges a game

explanation.surface: The crossword compiler pops by, keeping a judge away from his watchman duties.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Setter' seems to be the crossword's compiler, but it is the jam-setting agent PECTIN; without IN it is PECT, which holds REF.
explanation.definitionFit: A prefect is a senior pupil who acts as a monitor, keeping order in a school.

clue.text: Preserve carpenter (in a dream) and injure French invalid

parts.note: Peter Quince is the carpenter in Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream
to mar is to injure or spoil
malade is French for ill, an invalid

explanation.surface: A craftsman in a dream does harm to a sick Frenchman.
explanation.definitionFit: A fruit spread made from quinces is a type of preserve, like jam.

clue.text: Number in district where people fight

indicators.note: in places the number within the district

parts.note: an area is a district

explanation.surface: A figure in a part of town where there is brawling.
explanation.definitionFit: An arena is the enclosed ground where gladiators or combatants fought.

clue.text: Make heated and dry?

indicators.note: make in the sense of build or form, so the letters of the following words are formed anew

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Heat something until it is parched.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make' rearranges HEATED and DRY; the whole clue also describes what drying out by heat does.
explanation.definitionFit: To dehydrate is to remove water, which heating something until dry accomplishes.

clue.text: Geordie resident perversely entertains Yorkshire leader

indicators.note: entertains means the jumbled resident takes the county's first letter in
perversely means the letters of resident turn out contrary, out of order
leader means only the opening letter of the county name is used

explanation.surface: A local inhabitant awkwardly plays host to a Yorkshire chief.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perversely' rearranges RESIDENT into TNESIDER, and 'entertains' slips Y inside after the T.
explanation.definitionFit: A Geordie is a native of Newcastle and the surrounding area along the River Tyne in north-east England.

clue.text: Spotted snake's head at giant's village — inside was good enough

indicators.note: inside means the snake's head and village go within the word for sufficed

parts.note: did, as in 'that did', means sufficed

indicators.note: head means just the first letter of snake is wanted

parts.note: Cerne Abbas is a Dorset village famous for its huge chalk figure of a giant, shortened here to Cerne

explanation.surface: A snake was seen by the giant's village and found itself welcome indoors.
explanation.walkthrough: The Cerne Abbas giant is a famous chalk hill figure in Dorset, England.
explanation.definitionFit: To discern is to perceive or spot, so discerned means spotted.

clue.text: Faked evidence of factory growth

definitions.meaning: a living thing that grows, such as a shrub

explanation.surface: Forged proof of how a works grew.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means planted false evidence, an industrial works, and a growing organism.

clue.text: Columns arranged as fairies would do it?

parts.note: a peri is a fairy in Persian mythology
'as ... would do it' asks for a manner of doing, a style

explanation.surface: Pillars set up in the way that little folk would manage it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'as fairies would do it' reads as PERI STYLE, the fairy fashion.
explanation.definitionFit: A peristyle is a row of columns arranged around a courtyard or building.

clue.text: Holy man in charge of a kirk

indicators.note: in charge suggests something held in the keeping of the following words, concealed within them

explanation.surface: A clergyman put in control of a Scottish church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in charge of' looks like a job description; the letters sit inside 'of a kirk'. A kirk is a Scottish church.
explanation.definitionFit: A fakir is a Muslim or Hindu religious ascetic, a holy man who lives on alms.

clue.text: Crumbly as chips?

parts.note: the word read in two halves suggests 'able to be cooked in a pan of hot fat', like chips

explanation.definitionFit: Friable means easily crumbled, and split up it suggests fit for the frying pan.

clue.text: Cutter gripping clothes: what happens if he cuts his finger?

definitions.text: what happens if he cuts his finger?

indicators.note: gripping means the weapon holds the clothing inside it

parts.note: a sword is a cutting weapon
wear means clothing, as in menswear

explanation.surface: A tailor holding garments wonders what comes out if he nicks his finger.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cutter' suggests a tailor, which also sets up the definition: an oath is what slips out after nicking a finger.
explanation.definitionFit: A curse word is what someone typically blurts out on hurting a finger.

clue.text: Stranger in Dyfed starving and on his last legs

indicators.note: in puts the stranger within what remains of the county
starving means unfed, so the letters f-e-d are dropped from the county name

parts.note: odder means stranger

explanation.surface: A newcomer in a Welsh county goes hungry and is close to the end.
explanation.walkthrough: Dyfed is a county in Wales; 'starving' removes FED to leave DY, around ODDER.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone doddery is shaky and feeble with age, close to being on their last legs.

clue.text: Not kind of weather for Freud to be at home?

parts.note: in means at home
Clement Freud was a British broadcaster, writer and politician, grandson of Sigmund

explanation.surface: Bad weather means Freud should stay indoors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Freud' points to Sigmund, but it is Clement Freud, the British radio wit and MP.
explanation.definitionFit: Inclement weather is harsh and unkind, rough and stormy.

clue.text: Good shots to point — will get to 50 in time

parts.note: E, east, is a point of the compass

indicators.note: will get to means the fifty arrives inside the period of time

parts.note: an age is a period of time
L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: Fine shots aimed at a target will reach fifty in due course.
explanation.walkthrough: In golf an eagle is a hole played two under par.
explanation.definitionFit: An eagle is a very good golf score, two strokes under par, so it stands for good shooting.

clue.text: Both appreciation and disapprobation are forbidden

parts.note: ta is British informal for thank you
boo is a cry of disapproval

explanation.surface: Both praise and criticism are banned.
explanation.definitionFit: Something taboo is prohibited by custom, banned from use or mention.

clue.text: Fiddle return of game

indicators.note: return of means the name of the game is read back to front

parts.note: darts is a pub game

explanation.surface: A swindle comes back from a match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fiddle' looks like a cheat, but it is a violin: a Strad is a Stradivarius.
explanation.definitionFit: A Strad, short for Stradivarius, is a famous violin, and fiddle is another word for violin.

clue.text: Fund-raising event by Banbury's leading characters

indicators.note: characters as letters of the alphabet, here the letters of the two words rearranged

parts.note: the town name plus its S, every letter used
taken as written

explanation.surface: A charity sale held by the leading lights of an Oxfordshire town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leading characters' looks like it asks for initial letters, but all of BANBURYS and LEADING are rearranged. Banbury is a market town in Oxfordshire.
explanation.definitionFit: A bring-and-buy sale is a charity event where people donate goods and buy others' to raise money.

clue.text: Old 16 about good man, one with brains

indicators.note: about means the old oath goes round the good man

parts.note: egad is an old-fashioned mild oath, the kind of word entry 16 describes
he is the pronoun for a man

explanation.surface: An old curse surrounds a fine fellow who is very clever.
explanation.definitionFit: An egghead is an intellectual, someone with plenty of brains.

clue.text: Some bowling by amateur to cover

parts.note: an over is a set of six balls bowled in cricket
lay means amateur, non-professional, as in a lay person

explanation.surface: A spell of bowling from a non-professional to keep things under wraps.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket an over is a series of six balls from one bowler.
explanation.definitionFit: To overlay is to cover one surface with a layer of something.
